interactions.label: Why is the presence or absence of tissue bridges the most important feature for

params.question: Why is the presence or absence of tissue bridges the most important feature for distinguishing an incised wound from a laceration?

answers.text: Tissue bridges indicate whether the wound is ante-mortem or post-mortem

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ante-mortem versus post-mortem determination relies on signs of vital reaction such as haemorrhage and inflammatory infiltrate, not on tissue bridges.

answers.text: Tissue bridges survive blunt force tearing but are cleanly severed by sharp weapons, directly identifying the force mechanism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tough structures like blood vessels and nerves are torn unevenly by blunt force and remain as bridges across a laceration, whereas a sharp-edged weapon severs everything cleanly. This single feature reliably separates the two wound types and points to the class of weapon used.

answers.text: Tissue bridges determine the depth of the wound and therefore its severity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tissue bridges are strands of intact tissue crossing the wound floor; they do not determine wound depth. Depth is measured independently and relates to force and weapon penetration.

answers.text: Tissue bridges indicate the direction from which force was applied

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Direction of force may sometimes be inferred from abrasion tags or bevelling of wound edges, not from tissue bridges. Bridges indicate force type (blunt versus sharp), not direction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the key distinction: in a laceration (blunt force), tougher structures survive the tearing and span the wound as tissue bridges. In an incised wound (sharp force), the blade severs everything cleanly. This feature directly identifies the causative mechanism.

Well done. Tissue bridges are the single most reliable feature for distinguishing blunt force lacerations from sharp force incised wounds — a distinction that determines weapon class and shapes the entire medico-legal opinion.

interactions.label: A forensic physician documents a femur fracture but writes 'bone injury — simple

params.question: A forensic physician documents a femur fracture but writes 'bone injury — simple hurt' in the medico-legal certificate. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita framework, what is the most significant consequence of this error?

answers.text: The treating surgeon will choose a less aggressive management plan based on the MLC

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The MLC is a medico-legal document used by investigators and courts. The treating surgeon's management follows clinical protocols, which are independent of the statutory category written in the certificate.

answers.text: The court will automatically reclassify the injury once the X-ray report is reviewed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no automatic reclassification mechanism. Courts rely on the MLC as expert medical opinion. An error in the certificate directly affects the charge that investigators can file.

answers.text: Investigators can only file a lesser charge, allowing a serious offence to be under-prosecuted

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A femur fracture qualifies as grievous hurt under BNS Section 118 (fracture or dislocation of bone). Writing 'simple hurt' restricts the charge to a lesser category, potentially letting a serious offence go under-prosecuted. This is exactly why the forensic physician's clinical accuracy carries real legal weight.

answers.text: The doctor will face criminal proceedings for falsifying a medical record

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While falsifying medical records is a criminal offence under the BNS, an honest classification error is more likely to weaken the prosecution's case than to result in criminal proceedings against the doctor. The primary consequence is under-prosecution of the accused.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the chain: clinical characterisation → statutory category → criminal charge. When the forensic physician miscategorises a grievous injury (femur fracture, BNS Section 118) as simple hurt, investigators are restricted to a lesser charge, and the serious offence goes under-prosecuted.

Exactly right. The chain runs from clinical finding to statutory category to charge. A miscategorisation at the first step constrains every step that follows — precise documentation is a medico-legal obligation, not just good practice.

interactions.label: Wound healing timelines can be used forensically to assess whether delayed or in

params.question: Wound healing timelines can be used forensically to assess whether delayed or inadequate medical treatment contributed to a patient's death following an injury.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually true. The video described three forensic purposes of wound healing timelines: (1) retrospective dating of injuries based on healing stage, (2) establishing the chain of causation between wound and death, and (3) assessing contributory negligence — whether poor wound management (delayed treatment, missed tetanus prophylaxis) contributed to the outcome.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. This is the third forensic purpose of wound healing timelines: identifying contributory negligence. If wound care was delayed, tetanus prophylaxis missed, or cleaning inadequate, the treating physician's failure to act can be named as a contributing cause of the fatal outcome. The other two purposes are retrospective injury dating and establishing the chain of causation.

params.question: Police submit a curved, single-edged blade and ask the forensic physician to state whether it is a kripan with constitutional protection or an offensive weapon under the Arms Act. What should the physician's report contain?

answers.text: A definitive classification of the blade as either a kripan or a prohibited weapon under the Arms Act 1959

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Classifying a weapon as a kripan (constitutionally protected) or a prohibited item under the Arms Act is a legal and judicial determination, not a medical one. The physician's report should not make this classification.

answers.text: The blade's physical characteristics and an opinion on whether it could produce the observed injuries on the victim

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The forensic physician should objectively describe the weapon's measurable features — length, curvature, edge type, weight — and give an opinion on whether it is capable of producing the injuries documented. The cultural, religious, and legal classification of the weapon is for the court to decide.

answers.text: An opinion on the cultural and religious significance of the blade based on its design

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cultural and religious classification lies entirely outside the forensic physician's domain of expertise. Including such an opinion oversteps the physician's role and can undermine the objectivity of the entire report.

answers.text: A recommendation on whether the accused should be charged with illegal weapon possession

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Recommending charges is the domain of investigators and prosecutors. The physician provides factual findings and expert opinion on injury causation. An opinion that stretches beyond what you can measure undermines the entire process.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the boundary: the forensic physician describes physical characteristics and injury-producing capacity. Whether the weapon is a kripan, a prohibited item, or falls under the Arms Act is a legal determination for the court, not a medical opinion.

Exactly. The forensic physician's strength lies in objectivity — describing what can be measured and connecting physical evidence to wound patterns. Legal and cultural classification is the court's responsibility.

interactions.label: During examination of a medico-legal specimen, you observe a wound with torn, ir

params.question: During examination of a medico-legal specimen, you observe a wound with torn, irregular margins, intact strands of tissue crossing the wound floor, and soil contamination at the base. Which injury type is this, and what does the contamination indicate?

answers.text: Incised wound; the soil entered the wound during post-injury exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incised wounds have clean, well-defined margins with no tissue bridges. The torn irregular edges and tissue bridges here clearly rule out an incised wound, regardless of the contamination.

answers.text: Abrasion; the soil pattern indicates a fall on rough ground

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Abrasions are superficial injuries confined to the epidermis, with no wound gap or tissue bridges. While abrasions can carry surface patterns from the causative surface, the deep wound with tissue bridges described here is not an abrasion.

answers.text: Laceration; the tissue bridges and contamination point to blunt force impact against a rough, contaminated surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Torn irregular margins and tissue bridges are the hallmarks of a laceration caused by blunt force. The soil in the wound floor indicates the injury occurred against a rough, contaminated surface, helping reconstruct the mechanism — exactly the kind of medico-legal inference FM14.9 requires.

answers.text: Contusion; the irregular edges indicate deep subcutaneous haemorrhage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A contusion involves haemorrhage beneath intact, unbroken skin — there is no wound gap and no visible edges. The presence of a wound with exposed tissue and bridges rules out contusion entirely.

overallFeedback.feedback: Focus on the two defining features: torn irregular margins (not clean or well-defined) and tissue bridges (strands of intact tissue crossing the wound). Together these identify a laceration. The soil at the wound base further indicates blunt force contact with a rough surface.

Well identified. Tissue bridges, irregular edges, and wound-floor contamination together point to a laceration from blunt force against a rough surface — a complete medico-legal inference from a single specimen.
